body_markdown:
A wall-mounted time clock works fine when everyone reports to the same building every morning. It stops working the moment a business adds a second job site, a home health aide who never sees an office, or a crew that starts the day at a client’s driveway instead of a shop floor.


That’s the exact moment a lot of growth-stage employers hit a wall with time and attendance. The office manager who used to walk over and glance at the clock now has to ask crew leads to text their hours, or trust a paper log that gets turned in three days late, or chase down a remote employee who forgot to note when a shift actually started. None of that is a staffing problem. It’s a capture problem, and it has a specific fix.


## When One Time Clock Stops Covering the Whole Workforce


Construction crews, home health visits, field service technicians, and multi-site retail or hospitality operations share a common trait: the workforce doesn’t sit still. Employees clock in from a job site, a client’s home, a satellite location, or a personal vehicle between stops. A single physical clock at headquarters can’t see any of that.


The usual workarounds (text messages, phone calls, handwritten sheets) create the same downstream problems every payroll cycle: manually re-entering hours, disputed start times, and no reliable way to confirm someone actually worked where they said they did. Buddy punching and simple guesswork creep in, and the person responsible for payroll ends up doing detective work instead of processing hours.


Growth-stage employers who solve this well aren’t buying a fancier clock. They’re adding a mobile capture method that can confirm identity and location away from a fixed point, paired with software that turns that data into accurate, payroll-ready hours without a manual handoff.


## What Mobile Clock-In Has to Prove


A punch from a job site or a client’s home has to answer two questions a punch at a wall clock answers automatically: who is this, and were they actually there. It also has to keep working when a rural job site or a basement unit has no signal.


Fixed clocks typically solve the identity question with a badge, PIN, fingerprint, or facial scan tied to one physical device. That approach doesn’t travel. A crew that moves between three sites in a week needs a way to verify a punch without shipping a clock to every location, and that’s where location-based mobile verification steps in as a practical alternative to hardware-bound biometric methods. A handful of states, including Illinois, place specific legal requirements on collecting biometric data, so any employer weighing biometric capture should confirm the rules in every state where the business operates before adopting fingerprint or facial recognition time clocks. That’s a legal-review question, not a software one, and specific to each state’s current requirements.


Connectivity is the other gap. A field crew working in an area with weak signal still needs its punch recorded accurately in the moment, instead of losing it because a network dropped.


## The Capture Layer Is Device and App Territory


Solving identity and location verification on a phone or tablet, and keeping a punch working through a connectivity gap, is specialized hardware and app engineering. That work belongs to PayClock, delivered through Lathem, an Asure company that has manufactured time and attendance hardware since 1919.


Lathem’s PayClock Mobile app runs on iOS and Android and lets employees clock in and out from a smartphone or tablet, with location tracking attached to every punch so a manager can confirm where a shift actually started. It also includes an offline mode, so a punch made in a spot without signal still gets recorded and syncs automatically once the device reconnects. For the specifics on supported devices, setup, and how the app behaves in the field, the PayClock Mobile time clock app page covers that ground directly.


That division of labor matters for growth-stage employers evaluating options: the device and app handle capture, and a separate layer of software handles what happens to that data next.


## Turning a Punch Into Payroll-Ready Hours


Once a punch exists, whether it came from a badge reader in a break room or a phone at a job site, it still has to get matched against a schedule, checked for exceptions, approved by a manager, and moved into payroll without someone retyping it. That’s the software layer, and it’s where Asure Time & Attendance and AsureCentral do the work.


Asure Time & Attendance receives punch data from remote, mobile, and multi-site capture methods, applies scheduling and exception rules, and syncs approved hours into Asure Payroll without manual re-entry. In AsureCentral, Luna AI works alongside those exception rules on genuinely routine matching, and escalates anything unresolved, like a punch with no matching shift or a shift running well past its scheduled end, to a manager for review rather than letting it sit in a queue until someone notices at payroll close.


Consider a construction company running four crews across three active job sites. A crew lead clocks in through PayClock Mobile from the site trailer each morning. That punch, with its location and timestamp, flows into Asure Time & Attendance, where the system checks it against the crew’s scheduled shift, flags anything that looks off (a punch outside the expected radius, a shift that runs long), and routes it to the site supervisor for a quick approval. Once approved, the hours sync into Asure Payroll on their own. Nobody is retyping a timecard from a text message at the end of the week.


## What to Check Before You Add Mobile Clock-In


A few questions are worth working through before rolling mobile or remote clock-in out across a growing workforce.


- Does the capture method confirm both identity and location, and does it keep working when a job site has no signal?
- Does the time and attendance software apply scheduling and overtime rules automatically, or does someone still have to review every punch by hand?
- Do approved hours move into payroll without a manual export or re-entry step?
- Have state-level requirements around biometric data or location tracking been checked for every state where employees work?
- Does the exception-handling process scale as more crews, sites, or remote employees get added, or does it get slower with each one?


For a fuller walkthrough of the evaluation and rollout sequence, How to Select and Implement Time and Attendance Software in Five Procedures for Growth-Stage Teams covers the process end to end.


## Getting Started


Growth-stage employers with field crews, remote workers, or multiple sites don’t need to choose between accurate time capture and a manageable payroll process. Lathem’s PayClock Mobile app handles verified capture in the field, and Asure Time & Attendance turns that data into scheduled, exception-checked, payroll-ready hours inside AsureCentral. Employers evaluating a move away from paper timecards and text-message hours can start by looking at how Asure Time & Attendance fits their current scheduling and payroll setup, and build out from there.
